```tsx
// Silently does nothing. The drag and the scroll both fight for the touch.
import { ScrollView, type ScrollViewInstance } from 'react-native'

const scrollRef = useRef<ScrollViewInstance>(null)
const drag = useDrag({ axis: 'x', deferTo: scrollRef })
```

Use RNGH's `LegacyScrollView` instead. Its wrapper puts the tag on the ref:

```tsx
// Works. The ref carries a handlerTag.
import { LegacyScrollView } from '@rootnative/impulse/gesture-handler'

const scrollRef = useRef<LegacyScrollView>(null)
const drag = useDrag({ axis: 'x', deferTo: scrollRef })
```

Don't use the `ScrollView` of the same subpath. That is Gesture Handler 3's
own `ScrollView`, and its wrapper gives the ref to React Native's component, so
the ref has no tag. The same holds for `FlatList`: use `LegacyFlatList`. Both
come from [`@rootnative/impulse/gesture-handler`](/gesture-handler), so this
doesn't add an RNGH import to your app.

Gesture Handler 3 marks `LegacyScrollView` and `LegacyFlatList` as deprecated,
together with the gesture builder that Impulse uses, so your editor can show
them struck through. They work in Gesture Handler 3.

> **WARNING — This is not a web-only problem**
>
> RNGH resolves relations in its shared code, so the behaviour is the same on
> iOS, Android, and web. A relation against React Native's scroll view, or
> against Gesture Handler 3's own `ScrollView`, does nothing on every platform.

Another Impulse hook's `ref` always carries a tag, so `deferTo: drag.ref` needs
none of this.

### What the warning cannot catch

The check reads the ref after the gesture mounts. Three outcomes:

| What the ref holds then | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| A gesture, or a component that owns one | Silent. The relation is installed. |
| A mounted component with no handler tag | **Warns.** This is the `ScrollView` case above. |
| Nothing yet | Silent, on purpose. |

The third row is the limit. A target that mounts in a **later** commit than
the gesture (behind a loading flag, for example) has an empty ref when the
check runs, and nothing checks it again. That case stays quiet even when the
ref is wrong.

Silence is the right answer there, not a guess. RNGH resolves relations again
when a handler mounts late, so a correct late-mounting relation is installed.
A warning there would report a defect that doesn't exist. A warning that fires
on correct code is worse than no warning, because you learn to ignore it.

## A component ref needs a cast

```tsx
import { type GestureReference } from '@rootnative/impulse'
import { LegacyScrollView } from '@rootnative/impulse/gesture-handler'

const scrollRef = useRef<LegacyScrollView>(null)

const drag = useDrag({
  axis: 'x',
  deferTo: scrollRef as unknown as GestureReference,
})
```

RNGH types a relation target as a ref to a component **type**, and `ref={}`
never produces that type. So a real `ScrollView` ref doesn't satisfy it.

Impulse copies RNGH's type exactly, on purpose. A wider type that accepts an
instance ref would remove the compile-time check that catches an upstream
change to the relation signature.

> **WARNING — This is a known gap, not a decision**
>
> A library that exists to absorb RNGH's traps must not pass this one through.
> It is recorded as open. The fix is a wider type here, or a corrected
> `GestureRef` upstream.

## Coexistence and composition are different things

**Coexistence** relates your gesture to one it doesn't own, and the options
live on the hook.

**Composition** relates gestures you do own, and it goes through
[`useGestures`](/composition).

`useGestures` doesn't accept coexistence options. Put them on the members.

---

# Threads and callbacks

Every Impulse callback runs on one of two threads, and **the name tells you
which**.

| Kind | Names | Thread |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Phase | `onBegin`, `onUpdate`, `onFinalize` | UI thread. They are worklets. |
| Intent | `onTap`, `onDoubleTap`, `onLongPress`, `onLongPressEnd`, `onDragStart`, `onDragEnd` | JS thread. |

A phase name says **when** in the gesture you are. An intent name says **what
happened**.

## Why the split is in the name

A frame-by-frame stream and a semantic event are different things. If you have
to ask "which thread is this?", you will guess wrong one day. A wrong guess
fails on the UI thread with an unhelpful message.

We rejected a `runOnJS: true` flag per hook. That flag makes the thread
invisible at the call site and pushes the question into the docs.

## Intent callbacks: Impulse owns the boundary

```tsx
const tap = useTap({
  onTap: (event) => {
    setSelected(event.x)   // plain React state. No scheduleOnRN.
  },
})
```

You write an ordinary function. Impulse inserts the `scheduleOnRN` boundary.

## Phase callbacks: you own the worklet

```tsx
const drag = useDrag({
  axis: 'x',
  onUpdate: (event) => {
    'worklet'
    opacity.value = 1 - Math.abs(event.translation.x) / 200
  },
})
```

Mark it with the `'worklet'` directive. It receives a worklet-safe payload and
runs on the UI thread, so it can write a shared value every frame without a
round trip.

If you forget the directive, Impulse warns once in development. The warning
names the hook and the callback. Without that warning, the first touch that
reaches the phase throws `Tried to synchronously call a Remote Function.
Called "anonymous"`, and that message names neither.

> **DANGER — Never close over JS-thread state in a worklet**
>
> Read a shared value, or cross back with `scheduleOnRN` from
> `react-native-worklets`. A captured plain variable goes stale or crashes. It
> does so on the UI thread, where the message tells you almost nothing.
>
> Don't use `runOnJS` from `react-native-reanimated`. Reanimated 4 re-exports
> that name from `react-native-worklets` and marks the re-export deprecated.

## A worklet captures the whole result

Reading a shared value inside a worklet captures the **root identifier**, not
the field:

```tsx
const drag = useDrag({ axis: 'x' })

// This worklet captures `drag`, not `drag.x`.
const style = useAnimatedStyle(() => ({
  transform: [{ translateX: drag.x.value }],
}))
```

`react-native-worklets` copies a captured object field by field, through
`Object.entries`. An RNGH gesture can't cross the thread boundary, so a plain
result would throw `[Worklets] Cannot copy value of type 'PanGesture'` at
render, from the pattern that every page on this site shows.

So every intent result hides `gesture` and `ref` from enumeration. Both are
still properties, and you read them as usual, so
`<GestureDetector gesture={drag.gesture}>` and every coexistence option are
unaffected. The copy skips them, and the shared values go across, which is all
a worklet needs.

> **NOTE — What this changes for you**
>
> Nothing in the code you write. One thing you may see: `gesture` and `ref`
> don't appear in `Object.keys`, in a spread, in `JSON.stringify`, or in a
> logged result. Read them by name.

## The asymmetry that keeps gestures stable

This part looks like an implementation detail, and it isn't.

**A JS-thread callback is never a gesture dependency.** Impulse routes it
through a stable identity, so an inline callback is free:

```tsx
// Safe. This does not rebuild the gesture on every render.
const tap = useTap({ onTap: () => setCount(count + 1) })
```

Without that, an inline callback would change the identity of the gesture on
every render. `<GestureDetector>` would then re-attach the gesture, and a
re-attach in the middle of a drag drops the drag.

**A worklet callback is always a gesture dependency.** It has to be. Worklets
capture a function as written. A swap of its body would leave the UI thread
with the serialized version, with no error and no stale-closure warning.

So Impulse handles the two in opposite ways, on purpose:

| Callback | Inline is free | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `onTap`, `onDragEnd`, … | Yes | Reached through a stable identity. |
| `onBegin`, `onUpdate`, `onFinalize` | **No** | A worklet must be captured as written. |

> **NOTE — Keep worklet callbacks stable yourself**
>
> If you pass a phase callback, define it outside the component, or wrap it so
> that its identity is stable. An inline worklet rebuilds the gesture on every
> render.

One exception: when you add or remove an intent callback, Impulse **does**
rebuild the gesture. RNGH inspects the callbacks it receives to decide which
thread they run on, so a change in whether `onTap` exists has to change the
gesture. A different function in the same slot doesn't.

## `isActive` is a shared value

```tsx
const tap = useTap({ onTap: select })

const style = useAnimatedStyle(() => ({
  opacity: tap.isActive.value ? 0.6 : 1,
}))
```

It is a shared value so a pressed state runs on the UI thread with no
re-render. A read of `.value` during render works, but it tells you only what
was true at the last commit.

> **WARNING — `isActive` does not mean the same thing in every hook**
>
> `useTap` and `useDoubleTap` set it at `onBegin`, while the finger is down.
> `useLongPress`, `useDrag`, `usePan`, `useSwipe`, `usePinch`, and `useRotate`
> set it at recognition, once the gesture started.
>
> `useDoubleTap`'s `isActive` is also `true` for every ordinary single tap on
> the view, so it is not a pressed state. See
> [`useDoubleTap`](/use-double-tap).
>
> Both readings are right for their own hook. The whole life of a tap is the
> touch, and a long press that flagged every touch would flag nothing useful.
> Check the page of the hook before you use it in UI.

## Escape hatch

[`useRawGesture`](/raw-gestures) does **not** insert a `scheduleOnRN` boundary
for you. There you build the gesture, so RNGH decides per callback, by the
presence of the `'worklet'` directive.

---

# Raw gestures

`useRawGesture` is the mechanism-level escape hatch. Use it for a recognizer
that Impulse doesn't model, or a configuration that Impulse doesn't expose.

```tsx
import { useRawGesture } from '@rootnative/impulse'
import { Directions, Gesture } from '@rootnative/impulse/gesture-handler'

const fling = useRawGesture(
  () => Gesture.Fling().direction(Directions.RIGHT).onEnd(onFling),
  [onFling],
  { deferTo: scrollRef },
)

return (
  <GestureDetector gesture={fling.gesture}>
    <View />
  </GestureDetector>
)
```

It takes a builder, a dependency list, and the coexistence options every hook
accepts.

## What Impulse still gives you

- **Gesture identity across renders**, so an inline option can't re-attach the
  gesture in the middle of a drag.
- **`alongside` / `blocks` / `deferTo` resolution**, so the three RNGH
  relations are still chosen by outcome rather than by method name.
- **A `ref`** other hooks can name in their own coexistence options.

## What you own instead

**The dependency list.** `build` runs only when `deps` change, and a stale
capture is a stale gesture. A worklet callback belongs in `deps`. A JS-thread
callback doesn't. Give it a stable identity first, and depend on that.

**The thread.** Impulse does **not** insert a `scheduleOnRN` boundary here.
RNGH decides per callback, by the presence of the `'worklet'` directive. It
warns in development when a gesture mixes the two. The intent hooks can own
that boundary, because they know what each callback means. This hook doesn't.

**The payload.** You get RNGH's flat event (`translationX`, `velocityY`,
`absoluteX`), not an intent-shaped one.

## Do not call relation methods in the builder

```tsx
// Wrong.
useRawGesture(
  () => Gesture.Fling().requireExternalGestureToFail(scrollRef),
  [],
)

// Right.
useRawGesture(() => Gesture.Fling(), [], { deferTo: scrollRef })
```

Pass them in `options`. RNGH's relation methods append to the config of a
gesture, and don't replace it. So a relation in the builder **and** in the
options installs the same reference twice. Impulse applies them exactly once,
inside the same memo that builds the gesture.

See [Coexistence](/coexistence) for what the three options mean.

## Accessibility

Nothing here is reachable by a screen reader or a keyboard, and Impulse can't
name a fallback for a gesture it didn't design. Whatever this gesture does
must be reachable another way: an `accessibilityActions` entry, or a visible
control.

## When to reach for it

Use an intent hook first. `useRawGesture` gives up intent-shaped payloads and
the owned thread boundary, which are two of the three reasons Impulse exists.

If you build the same raw gesture in more than one project, that is a gap in
Impulse. Report it.

---

# Gesture Handler interop

Impulse hides RNGH by default, and its intent hooks cover the common cases. For
the rest, this subpath re-exports RNGH's own primitives under their original
names:

```tsx
import { Directions, Gesture, State } from '@rootnative/impulse/gesture-handler'
```

So `@rootnative/impulse` stays your only gesture import. You don't add a
second import to reach a mechanism that Impulse doesn't model.

## These are pure re-exports

`Gesture.Pan()` reached through this subpath is **the same object** as
`Gesture.Pan()` reached from `react-native-gesture-handler`. A test pins that.

> **WARNING — None of Impulse's guarantees apply to what you build with it**
>
> The hooks of Impulse give you stable gesture identity, thread-explicit
> callbacks, and intent-shaped payloads. A bare RNGH gesture has none of them.
>
> To keep identity and coexistence while you build the gesture yourself, use
> [`useRawGesture`](/raw-gestures) instead of a bare `useMemo`.

## `GestureDetector` comes from the root entry

```tsx
import { GestureDetector } from '@rootnative/impulse'
```

You pass the result of every hook to it, so the package entry exports it. You
don't need this subpath to get it.

## Composing a raw gesture with Impulse hooks

A bare RNGH gesture is a valid [composition](/composition) member:

```tsx
import { Gesture } from '@rootnative/impulse/gesture-handler'
import { useGestures, useTap } from '@rootnative/impulse'

const fling = useMemo(() => Gesture.Fling(), [])
const tap = useTap({ onTap: select })

const { gesture } = useGestures([tap, fling], { mode: 'race' })
```

Use [`useRawGesture`](/raw-gestures) instead of the hand-written `useMemo`
above. It does the memoisation for you and accepts the coexistence options.

---

# Web behaviour

Web is a platform, not a footnote. RNGH's web implementation differs from its
native one. This page exists so that you don't discover that in each project.

> **NOTE — What "verified" means here**
>
> We ran each verified row in a desktop browser against the example app. We
> didn't check the rows marked **unverified**, and they are not claims.

## Status by intent

| Intent | Activation criteria honoured | Behaviour in a browser |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `useTap` | Yes, verified in RNGH's source | **Works** |
| `useDoubleTap` | Yes, verified in RNGH's source | **Works** |
| `useLongPress` | Yes, verified in RNGH's source | **Works**, with two limits below |
| `useDrag` | Yes, verified in RNGH's source | **Works** |
| `usePan` | Yes, verified in RNGH's source | **Unverified** |
| `useSwipe` | Yes, verified in RNGH's source | **Unverified** |
| `usePinch` | No criteria to honour | **Unverified**, and a trackpad can't drive it. See below |
| `useRotate` | No criteria to honour | **Unverified**, and a trackpad can't drive it. See below |

The first four intents recognize correctly under a mouse on web. We didn't run
the last four in a browser, so their rows are not claims.

## A mouse cannot drive a two-finger intent

RNGH recognizes pinch and rotation from pointer events, so both need **two
pointers**: a touchscreen, or a device that reports them. One mouse is one
pointer, so neither hook fires under it at all.

A trackpad doesn't close the gap. Its pinch arrives as a `wheel` event with
`ctrlKey`, and its rotation arrives as a platform gesture event. Neither is a
pointer pair, so neither reaches these hooks. So a desktop browser with only a
trackpad can't zoom or turn.

Give both a control that writes `scale` or `angle` directly. The accessibility
fallbacks of [`usePinch`](/use-pinch#accessibility) and
[`useRotate`](/use-rotate#accessibility) need that control anyway. The
browser's own page zoom is unaffected in both cases.

We read this in RNGH's web implementation and didn't measure it. That is why
the two rows above still say unverified.

## The cancel path reports on the JS thread

We found this during the web pass, and it is **not a web-specific problem**.
It behaves the same on a device.

Hold a `useLongPress` past `minDuration`. Then move the pointer more than
`maxDistance` (10 points by default) without a release. RNGH cancels the
press, and `onLongPressEnd` reports it:

```tsx
const hold = useLongPress({
  onLongPress: () => setPhase('held'),
  onLongPressEnd: (event, { cancelled }) => {
    setPhase(cancelled ? 'cancelled' : 'released')
  },
})
```

Every end callback works this way: `onTap`, `onDoubleTap`, `onLongPressEnd`,
and `onDragEnd`. Each fires on both endings, and `cancelled` says which. See
[the cancel path](/use-long-press#the-cancel-path) for the full contract.

Before this argument existed, only `onFinalize` reported a cancel, and
`onFinalize` is a worklet. So a screen that held its phase in React state had
to write `'worklet'` plus `scheduleOnRN` by hand. That is the ceremony that
Impulse exists to remove, and it is gone.

`onFinalize` is unchanged. It fires for every touch that reached the view,
recognized or not. That makes it the right place to undo what `onBegin` set.

## `useLongPress` cancels on travel, against RNGH's own contract

RNGH documents `maxDist` as bounding the wait only — *"if the finger travels
further than the defined distance **and the handler hasn't yet activated**, it
will fail"*. A recognized press should tolerate travel.

Its web implementation doesn't do that. `checkDistanceFail()` runs on every
pointer move, and when the gesture is already active, it calls `cancel()`.

So on web, a move past `maxDistance` during a hold ends the press. **Native is
unverified.** RNGH's documentation says travel is allowed there, so this may
be a real platform split.

The practical cost: **hold-then-drag doesn't work on web at the default
`maxDistance`.** The movement of the drag cancels the press that gates it.
Raise `maxDistance` explicitly for that pattern. Don't rely on the documented
behaviour.

## Coexistence on web

A relation needs a ref that carries a `handlerTag`, and that rule comes from
RNGH's shared code, not its platform code. So a relation against React
Native's `ScrollView`, or Gesture Handler 3's own `ScrollView`, does nothing
on web **and** on native.

See [Coexistence](/coexistence) for the working form.

## Known unknowns

These are open questions. We record them so the list is honest, not empty.

- **Touch screens and trackpads.** The pass above used a mouse. We didn't
  check a trackpad or a touch screen.
- **The browser's own gestures.** Text selection, press-and-hold context menus,
  and pull-to-refresh all compete for the same input. We checked no intent
  against them.
- **Mobile browsers.** We checked nothing on iOS Safari or Android Chrome, and
  those are the browsers most likely to differ.
- **The jsdom test per intent.** Principle 8 asks for one per intent. None
  exists.

## How to run the survey

```bash
pnpm run example:web
```

Then open each screen. Record what happens. An intent that you didn't test is
unverified, not working.

---

# Testing

Impulse ships its own Jest wiring, so you need one line.

```js
// jest.config.js
module.exports = {
  preset: require.resolve('@rootnative/impulse/jest-preset'),
}
```

The setup, and the `@react-native/jest-preset` devDependency it needs, are on
the [Installation](/installation) page. This page is about what you can and
can't assert once it runs.

## Render inside the root view

Gesture Handler 3 throws when a `<GestureDetector>` renders outside a
`<GestureHandlerRootView>`. Jest runs with `__DEV__` set, so a test gets the
same error as a development build. Pass the root view as the `wrapper` of each
render:

```tsx
import { render } from '@testing-library/react-native'
import { GestureHandlerRootView } from 'react-native-gesture-handler'

render(<Card />, { wrapper: GestureHandlerRootView })
```

A test that only calls `renderHook` needs no wrapper, because it renders no
`<GestureDetector>`.

## Driving a gesture

Use RNGH's own helpers. Don't simulate raw touch events by hand.

Tag the gesture so the helper can find it:

```tsx
const tap = useTap({ testId: 'card', onTap: select })
```

```tsx
import {
  fireGestureHandler,
  getByGestureTestId,
} from 'react-native-gesture-handler/jest-utils'

fireGestureHandler(getByGestureTestId('card'))
```

Every hook accepts `testId`, and forwards it to RNGH's `withTestId`.

## Asserting configuration

The activation criteria of a hook are on the gesture object, so you can assert
them without a render:

```tsx
const { result } = renderHook(() => useTap())

expect(result.current.gesture.config.maxDurationMs).toBe(500)
expect(result.current.gesture.config.maxDist).toBe(10)
```

This is how Impulse pins its own defaults, and it is the most precise check
available. It asks what configuration the gesture received, not what the mock
did with it.

## What the mock can and cannot do

The preset mocks Reanimated and `react-native-worklets`, and the mocks are
thin on purpose. Neither real module runs under Jest: Reanimated loads
`react-native-worklets`, and worklets needs its native module.

Impulse crosses to the JS thread with `scheduleOnRN` from
`react-native-worklets`, so both mocks are necessary. If you remove either
one, every intent test fails at import.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| ✅ | Assert a shared value's `.value` after driving a gesture |
| ✅ | Assert that a JS-thread callback fired: the mock's `scheduleOnRN` calls it synchronously |
| ✅ | Assert a gesture's configuration |
| ❌ | Frame-level timing. Nothing schedules or animates |

The mock **leaves out** `useAnimatedStyle`, the `Animated.*` components, and
the animation functions, on purpose. Impulse renders none of them and starts
no animation. If your own test needs them, add them in your own setup.

## Three things the mock cannot see

Each of these needs a check another way. More Jest won't close any of them.

### 1. Gesture identity

`<GestureDetector>` re-attaches a gesture whose identity changes, and a
re-attach in the middle of a drag drops the drag. The mock can't see this, so
assert it directly:

```tsx
const first = result.current.gesture
rerender({ onTap: () => {} })     // a different inline callback
expect(result.current.gesture).toBe(first)
```

Impulse pins this in `gestureIdentity.test.tsx` across an inline callback, an
inline coexistence array, a handler that appears and disappears, and a
composition. It also pins the worklet case in the other direction, where
identity **must** change.

If you build gestures with [`useRawGesture`](/raw-gestures), this is the test to
copy. You own the dependency list there.

### 2. Frame-level correctness and platform activation

A test runner can't tell you whether a horizontal drag inside a vertical
`ScrollView` feels right, or whether a 10-point threshold is the right number.

That is what the example app is for, and **a device pass is a release
requirement, not an option.**

### 3. A gesture that fails before it activates

> **DANGER — This one produces tests that pass for the wrong reason**
>
> `fireGestureHandler` fills the state sequence of every gesture from
> `[BEGAN, ACTIVE, END]`. It injects an ACTIVE event with its own default payload
> **before** any FAILED that you give it, so `onStart` always runs.
>
> A long press released after 50 ms still reaches `onLongPress` under the mock. A
> drag that never passed its threshold still starts.

So you can't assert `useDrag`'s `threshold` and `useLongPress`'s `minDuration`
by behaviour. Assert them against the **config** of the gesture instead, as
above.

Any intent whose JS-thread callback fires at `onStart` inherits this.

## Pure functions

Payload normalizers and relation resolution are plain functions. Test them
directly, with no render. That is faster, and the failure points at the right
line.

## Web

Web behaviour gets its own jsdom Jest project, mirroring the native/web split.

> **NOTE — Not built yet**
>
> Principle 8 asks for a jsdom test per intent. None exists. We did the
> [web survey](/web) by hand in a browser, and no test pins its findings.

---

# AI agents and `llms.txt`

A coding agent that writes against Impulse has two failure modes: it invents a
hook that doesn't exist, or it describes a version that isn't the installed
one. These files exist to close both.

| File | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| [`/llms.txt`](pathname:///impulse/llms.txt) | A concise overview: the surface, the defaults, and the traps. Hand-written. |
| [`/llms-full.txt`](pathname:///impulse/llms-full.txt) | Every page on this site, in sidebar order. Generated. |

## Prefer the installed copy

`llms.txt` also ships inside the package:

```
node_modules/@rootnative/impulse/llms.txt
```

**That copy is the exact API of the version in the project.** Use it instead
of anything hosted. This site describes the last release, and that may not be
the version an app installed. During alpha those differ often.

The package also ships its own `src`, so an agent can read the real
implementation instead of inferring it.

## What the overview leads with

Not the feature list. The things that fail silently, because an agent can't
discover those from its own output:

- `useHover` and `useEdgeSwipe` are **designed and not written**. They appear
  in the design documents. They are not importable.
- `useRotate` reports **degrees**, not the radians RNGH reports. It is the one
  place Impulse changes a unit, and an agent that passes `Math.PI / 4` as a
  bound writes a range 40 times too wide.
- `usePan` and `useDrag` are different hooks, and an agent that treats them as
  synonyms writes the wrong one. `useDrag` owns a position that accumulates,
  and `bounds` clamps it. `usePan` owns nothing and reports a per-frame
  `change` that you add up.
- RNGH drops a relation against React Native's `ScrollView`, or Gesture
  Handler 3's own `ScrollView`, because the ref carries no `handlerTag`. Use
  `LegacyScrollView` or `LegacyFlatList` from
  `@rootnative/impulse/gesture-handler`. Impulse warns once in development
  when the ref is filled before the gesture mounts. It can't see the case
  where the ref is filled later.
- A missing `<GestureHandlerRootView>` means gestures never fire. In
  development on iOS and Android, and in Jest, Gesture Handler 3 throws an
  error that names the root view. On web and in a release build the console
  stays empty.
- A tap and a double tap compose `exclusive` with the double tap first. `race`
  fails quietly.

## Regenerating

```bash
pnpm run build:llms
```

`docs/static/llms.txt` is **written by hand** and is the source. The script
copies it into the package and builds `llms-full.txt` from the pages, in the
order `docs/sidebars.ts` gives.

Run it again after you edit a page or change the public API. CI fails on a
dirty diff over the generated files, and `check:artifact` fails if `llms.txt`
is missing from the published tarball.

---

# Roadmap

Impulse is at `0.0.0-alpha.2`. This page says what exists, so nothing on this
site reads as a promise.

## What ships today

| | Hook | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ✅ | [`useTap`](/use-tap) | A single tap |
| ✅ | [`useDoubleTap`](/use-double-tap) | Two taps in quick succession |
| ✅ | [`useLongPress`](/use-long-press) | A press held past a duration |
| ✅ | [`useDrag`](/use-drag) | A drag, streaming where it is |
| ✅ | [`usePan`](/use-pan) | A pan, streaming how the finger moved |
| ✅ | [`useSwipe`](/use-swipe) | A pan judged at release, with a direction |
| ✅ | [`usePinch`](/use-pinch) | A two-finger pinch that owns its scale |
| ✅ | [`useRotate`](/use-rotate) | A two-finger rotation, in degrees |
| ✅ | [`useGestures`](/composition) | Composition under one relation |
| ✅ | [`useRawGesture`](/raw-gestures) | The mechanism-level escape hatch |
| ✅ | [`alongside` / `blocks` / `deferTo`](/coexistence) | Coexistence, on every hook |

## Designed, not written

**Don't import these.** They are decisions, not features that exist.

`useHover` · `useEdgeSwipe`

## Milestones

### 1 — The composition and coexistence core

The hard part, built first, because every intent depends on it.

**The code is complete. The mechanical half of the gate passes. The feel half
has no result.**

> _Gate:_ a horizontal `useDrag` inside a vertical `ScrollView` works on iOS and
> Android hardware, and a `useTap` / `useDoubleTap` race resolves correctly.
> Verified on a device, not in Jest.

**A device sweep ran on 2026-09-19 and 2026-09-20**, on an Android emulator
with injected touches and on an iOS simulator with XCUITest. Both checks passed
on both platforms:

- A horizontal `useDrag` row opens to exactly its target of 120 points. A
  vertical drag that starts on a row scrolls the list, with no relation
  declared.
- The race resolves. Below `maxDelay`, two taps gave one double tap and no
  single tap. Above it, two taps gave two single taps and no double tap.

**The sweep doesn't measure feel**, and no physical device ran it. So each
activation-criteria default on this site is still a design intention, and
each page says what the sweep proved and what it didn't.

### 2 — The intent set

Eight of ten intents exist. Each one needs a screen, a docs page, and a device
pass. The device sweep drove all eight on at least one platform. None of them
has a feel result.

- **Written, tested, documented, and on a screen:** `useTap`, `useDoubleTap`,
  `useLongPress`, `useDrag`, `usePan`, `useSwipe`, `usePinch`, `useRotate`.
- **Designed only:** `useHover`, `useEdgeSwipe`.

### 3 — The Inertia bridge

`@rootnative/impulse/inertia` adapts a release payload into the release
transitions of [`@rootnative/inertia`](https://rootnative.github.io/inertia/).

It will be an **optional** subpath. Impulse will never require an animation
library. That is the reason it is a separate package.

> _Gate:_ a swipe-to-dismiss row and a pinch-to-zoom viewer built from Impulse
> plus Inertia, with no gesture-handler or Reanimated import in the consumer
> code.

## Known gaps

The gaps you can hit:

- **RNGH drops a relation against React Native's `ScrollView`, or Gesture
  Handler 3's `ScrollView`.** The ref carries no `handlerTag`, so RNGH
  installs nothing. Impulse warns once in development when it can see the
  problem, which is when the ref is filled before the gesture mounts. A target
  that mounts later stays silent. Use RNGH's `LegacyScrollView`. See
  [Coexistence](/coexistence).
- **A missing `<GestureHandlerRootView>` fails silently on web and in a release
  build.** In development on iOS and Android, Gesture Handler 3 throws an error
  that names the root view. Impulse adds no warning of its own, because RNGH
  doesn't export the context that would let it detect a missing root view.
- **Impulse reports a cancel, but the velocity that comes with it is not a
  throw.** Every end callback fires on both paths and carries `cancelled`. The
  finger never lifted on the cancelled path, so a spring on `velocity` flings
  a view that the finger never released. See [Web behaviour](/web).
- **A relation target needs a cast.** RNGH types it as a ref to a component
  *type*, and `ref={}` doesn't produce that type.
- **`useLongPress`'s `maxDistance` cancels an active press on web**, against
  RNGH's own documented contract. Hold-then-drag doesn't work there at the
  default.
- **No activation default has a feel result.** The device sweep proved that
  some defaults work: the drag threshold, `useSwipe`'s `commitDistance` of 80
  points, and `maxDelay` at 500 ms and 250 ms. It didn't prove that any of
  them feels right. `useSwipe`'s `commitSpeed` of 800 points per second is not
  tested, because neither harness can make a swipe that is short enough and
  fast enough. `usePinch` and `useRotate` add no default, because neither RNGH
  recognizer exposes a threshold. So their coexistence rests on a relation
  alone.
- **`usePinch`'s `elastic` has no recommended value.** `useDrag` defaults it to
  `0` and the example screen invented `0.35`. Impulse also computes the
  resistance on the scale, not on its logarithm. So a pull below `min` resists
  differently from a pull above `max` by the same factor. Only a hand can tell
  whether that feels wrong.
- **Web is surveyed by hand, not by tests.** No jsdom test exists for any
  intent.

## Out of scope indefinitely

These are not "later". They are decisions.

- **Components.** No `<Swipeable>`, no drawer, no carousel. A component makes
  layout and styling decisions that a gesture library must not make.
- **An animation vocabulary.** No springs, no transitions, no easing. Hooks
  return values; the consumer animates them.
- **A design system.** No haptics policy, no platform-conditional feel.
- **Solving keyboard accessibility for gestures.** Impulse names the fallback on
  every intent page. It doesn't invent a keyboard gesture model.

## Before `1.0.0`

We must validate the API against **one component library and one independent
application**. Neither has to be ours, and the example app doesn't count.

An API co-designed with its only consumer can't show the assumptions the two
share. A major version lock makes shared assumptions permanent.

`1.0.0` is the API stability lock, not a quality signal.
